listenings.text: Morning report for tomorrow. The swell arrives overnight, about one and a half metres, which is good. The problem is the wind. Early it is light and offshore, so if you are in the water before eight you will get the best of it. After nine it swings onshore and it gets choppy, and if the gusts are as strong as the model says, it will be unsurfable by eleven. Tide is low at six twenty, so expect closeouts on the inside bank first thing. Flags go up at seven. And one last thing: if the swell is bigger than forecast, the north end will be the safe option.

So this is how I decide, and it takes me about thirty seconds. First, if the wind is onshore, I do not even get out of bed, because it is never worth it. Second, if the tide is under half a metre I skip it too, because it closes out and I just get tired. If both of those are fine, I look at the flags on the webcam, and if they are red I stay home, obviously. And then the last one, which is the only one that changes: if I have an assignment due the next day, I go anyway and I do the assignment at eleven at night. I have never once chosen the assignment.

items.situation: Explain when a wave is a closeout, and what you do about it.

reading.rtitle: How a surfer reads a forecast
paras: A forecast is not a promise. It is a list of conditions, and every experienced surfer turns that list into a set of if-sentences before breakfast.

Start with the wind, because the wind decides everything. If the wind is offshore, the waves are clean and everybody is happy. If it is onshore, the water gets choppy and most people stay in bed. Gusts matter too: if there are strong gusts, even a good swell falls apart.

Then the tide and the sandbank. If the tide is too low, the waves break all at once and you get closeouts. If the sandbank has moved after a storm, the whole spot changes and yesterday's knowledge is worth nothing.

Then the safety line, which is not negotiable. If the flags are red, nobody goes in. Not experienced surfers, not locals, nobody. On a big day over a reef it is risky even for people who have surfed there for years.

And finally the decision, which is always about one specific morning. If it is onshore tomorrow, I will stay home and do my assignment. If the swell arrives on time, I will be in the water before sunrise. That is the whole system, and it takes about forty seconds.
